html:
The Pataxó are an Indigenous people of southern Bahia in Brazil, on the coast around Porto Seguro and Monte Pascoal. Today they number about 12,000.

Their coast is where the Portuguese first came ashore in Brazil, in the landing of Cabral in 1500, and it was settled early. Over the next centuries the Pataxó were pushed into the forests behind the coast, alongside the Maxakalí and other peoples whom the Portuguese lumped together as Aimoré or Botocudo. Farms took most of their land. In 1951 a police attack on their village of Barra Velha scattered them, and in 1961 they were expelled from the forest of the new Monte Pascoal national park.

Many settled on the coast instead, founding villages such as Coroa Vermelha in 1972. Their old language fell out of use; they now speak Portuguese and are rebuilding a language called Patxohã. Their homeland was once Tupinambá and Tupiniquim country on the shore.
sum: The Pataxó are an Indigenous people of southern Bahia in Brazil, on the coast around Porto Seguro and Monte Pascoal. Today they number about 12,000.
